column6: The commentary condemns driving a beast beyond its strength; Jacob warns Esau that nursing flocks and herds would all die if driven hard for even one day.

column5: pace matched to livestock and children
column6: The commentary's good rider respects the mount's capacity; Jacob promises to proceed slowly at the pace of the livestock and children in his care.
The commentary makes animal care a concrete good action; this command requires returning even an enemy's lost ox or donkey instead of abandoning it on the route.

column5: Moses asked to carry people like infant
column6: The commentary portrays the human as a load bearer; Moses asks whether he conceived the people, since God has told him to carry them like a nurse carrying a child to the promised land.
The commentary warns against a load exceeding its bearer; God promises that the elders will bear the burden of the people with Moses so he will not carry it alone.

column5: God seeks camp and shows the way
column6: The commentary's trustworthy travel depends on a passable route; Moses says God went before Israel to find camping places and show the way by night and day.
The commentary turns loss into a weight borne on the journey; the servant bears others' griefs and carries their sorrows, specifying a load distinct from the iniquities in Isaiah 53:11.

column5: shouldered idol cannot move or answer
column6: The commentary asks what a carrier's load can do for him; worshippers bear an idol on the shoulder and set it down, but it cannot move or answer their cry.
The commentary joins inner trust to a traversable way; this blessing gives strength to the pilgrim whose heart holds the highways to Zion.

column5: hard valley becomes a place of springs
column6: The commentary's difficult route must be endured rather than merely named; pilgrims crossing the valley of Baca make it a place of springs.

column5: pilgrims go from strength to strength
column6: The commentary's traveler needs endurance up to the destination; the psalm has pilgrims advancing from strength to strength toward Zion.

column5: wanderers find no road to city
column6: The commentary makes the human a traveler whose outcome matters; wanderers in the wilderness cannot find a way to an inhabited city.
The commentary's rider or walker can be exhausted by the route; the same wanderers grow hungry and thirsty until their lives faint within them.
The commentary's beaten road points toward an end; God leads the lost wanderers by a straight way until they reach an inhabited city.
The commentary praises a mount that does not stumble and an opened path; God leads the returning people beside water on a straight road where they will not stumble.
The commentary's dependable carrier does not trip despite continued travel; wisdom promises that a walker's steps will not be cramped and that a runner will not stumble.
The commentary makes legs and endurance part of the steep way; the prophet tells the community to strengthen weak hands and make feeble knees firm before the promised return.

column5: up the mountain to learn ways
column6: The commentary joins a mountain ascent to righteous travel; the nations invite one another up the Lord's mountain so they may learn his ways and walk in his paths.

column5: who may dwell on holy hill
column6: The commentary's mountain is a destination that tests the traveler; this verse asks who may dwell on God's holy hill, giving the destination for the ethical walker of Psalm 15:2.

column5: good works prepared as a way to walk
column6: The commentary places good action on the human journey; the letter says people are created for good works prepared beforehand so that they may walk in them.

column5: worthy walk bearing good work's fruit
column6: The commentary joins a right road to effective work; the letter asks believers to walk worthily while bearing fruit in every good work.

column5: Jesus endures cross for joy ahead
column6: The commentary's bearer must endure a difficult route to its outcome; the runner is directed to Jesus, who endured the cross for the joy set before him.
The commentary praises a carrier who does not grow weary; Hebrews asks readers to consider Jesus' endurance of hostility so they themselves do not tire or lose heart.

column5: work and labor not in vain
column6: The commentary asks whether human labor ends in loss; Paul urges steadfast work for the Lord on the ground that such labor is not in vain.

column5: running and laboring not in vain
column6: The commentary combines the road, human work, and the danger of loss; Paul hopes at Christ's day to find that he neither ran nor labored in vain.
The commentary's trusted mount and good treatment put confidence beside action; Paul describes effective faith as working through love.

column5: Moses and people wear out under heavy task
column6: The commentary warns that even a willing bearer has a limit; Jethro tells Moses that he and the people will wear out because the judging burden is too heavy for one person.
The commentary's overloading image calls for a changed distribution; Jethro proposes other judges handle smaller cases and share Moses' burden.
The commentary makes a beast both load bearer and support for travelers; Joseph sends loaded male and female donkeys with goods and food for his father's journey.
The commentary explicitly attends to the human side used for mounting; Rebekah gets down from her camel on seeing Isaac, though this verse does not name a side.
The commentary notices the physical relation between rider and mount; Abigail quickly gets down from her donkey when she meets David, though the side is unspecified.
The commentary turns a repeatedly trodden path into moral action; the psalmist proposes to run the way of God's commandments when his heart is enlarged.
The commentary's traveler and reliable animal must resist exhaustion; God gives power to the faint and increases strength for those without it before the running and walking of Isaiah 40:31.
The commentary considers the rider's character through his mount; following the humble king's donkey, the prophecy removes warhorses and announces peace.

column5: mountain ascent to learn walking paths
column6: The commentary joins a steep destination to the way of right action; Micah's parallel oracle has nations ascend God's mountain to learn his ways and walk his paths.
The commentary joins a beast and a steep road in the endurance image; Habakkuk names the failure of flocks and herds before speaking of feet fitted for the heights.
The commentary's journey is evaluated by response to loss; after listing failed crops and absent animals, Habakkuk resolves to rejoice in God before describing his strengthened feet.
The commentary calls kindness to a strained beast good action; the rabbinic discussion permits placing cushions to help an animal fallen into a pit because of its suffering.

column5: first aid even for enemy's beast
column6: The commentary tests a rider's goodness by the animal's welfare; the discussion gives priority to helping an enemy's animal in order to subdue hostility, a reason distinct from relieving animal suffering.
The commentary's human carries a moral load along a path; after urging the pupil to shoulder wisdom, Sirach says to follow her ways with all one's strength.
The commentary asks which burden is fitting for a person; the teacher invites pupils to put their necks under wisdom's yoke and receive instruction.
The commentary links exertion on a hard route to its result; the teacher says he labored a little and found much rest in wisdom.
The commentary distinguishes a reliable animal from a human traveler; Jesus himself is wearied by his journey and sits beside a well.
The commentary's burden image implies attention to what another can carry; Paul asks the strong to bear the weaknesses of those without strength.
The commentary opposes driving a creature under an intolerable load; this letter says God's commands are not burdensome for the loving believer.

column5: light affliction and weight of glory
column6: The commentary weighs a journey's burden against its final outcome; Paul sets momentary light affliction beside the immense lasting weight of glory it produces.
The commentary makes the human a burden bearer facing mortality; Paul describes people in an earthly tent as groaning while burdened and awaiting life beyond mortality.

column5: lawyers impose burdens they will not touch
column6: The commentary condemns forcing another beyond capacity; Jesus says legal experts load people with hard burdens while refusing to touch the loads themselves.
The commentary makes good treatment of a traveler concrete; the letter commends faithful work for visiting brothers, including strangers, before urging their onward journey.
The commentary contrasts an exhausting load with one that can be carried; this saying invites people under an easy yoke and promises rest, a second Christian form of the burden image.
The commentary makes kindness to an animal a good act; after the sheep-in-a-pit example, Jesus says doing good on the Sabbath is lawful and compares human worth with the sheep's.
The commentary distinguishes a fitting load from excessive demands; the speaker says he lays no other burden on the faithful hearers at Thyatira.
The commentary's bearer needs patience through the whole way; the next verse tells those hearers to hold fast what they have until the speaker comes.
The commentary's human road can lead to loss; after the claim that Christ bore sins, Peter calls his readers wandering sheep now returned to their shepherd.
